title: Excelsior and Onward bands: instrumentation and marching in step
summary: Ernie recalls the Excelsior and Onward bands, with their large instrumentation, constant rehearsal and every player stepping off together on the first beat, discipline he says is gone.

story.theme_name: Brass bands, parades and jazz funerals
story.community_name: Parading for Mardi Gras and the clubs

blocks.x: In other words, he kept all the music and everything. He was a good reader. Strictly most of the reader. He had the Eureka. Yeah, he enjoyed that Eureka then. He was really Carnage in the band then on Trinidad. No, Willie had died. He was out of there then. He was out of there. But I'm more sure that Landry had played with Carnage. He had been a member of the Eureka. Yeah, yeah, yeah. For a long time. He and Rodgers both. He and Ernest Rodgers both. He's been members of Eureka for years. I never had a chance to play with the original Excelsior. In fact, I wasn't playing trumpet at that time because the leader of that band was George Morett. And I think he died in the early 20s. Willie Parcher was in that band. Yeah, he was in that band. Excelsior brass band. And the Ormond brass band, that was Manuel Perez with Teo and Eddie Jackson and Bill Matthews, brother. Bill Matthews. Big Eddie used to come through us too. That was the band. That was my band, that Ormond.
Did that Ormond come through? That's the move.

I didn't like to go. That's right. Of course, the Excelsior was a wonderful band, but I mean they were more musical. Not that they were better musicians because none of the bands had more music than me. They were well voiced with the instruments, see. Like today, you get a band that got them to play a funeral, you get three trumpets, two drums, a clarinet and a saxophone, two trombones and a bass. And that's all they got. Excelsior and them, they had two trombones and a bass on them, and they had an upright alto and a mellophone. And they had a baritone and an E-flat clarinet. And then the saxophones fall behind it, three trumpets, and in fact they carried 12, 14, 15 pieces. Well, quite natural, when they put that music in front of them, you got more instrumentation, you can have more voices, the band is heavy. And they all play and they rehearsals so much, it's so perfect. I mean, you just got to stand up and listen at it. And another thing that they did in those days that they don't do now because I imagine the competition caused it. When that bass drum would hit off for them to start playing, everybody in that band, when they would step down, everybody's foot would step together. That was their first count. When their foot come down and the other foot come down, they hit together on their first beat. And they stood like that until that number was over. That went for the original U-Ricka, Hornwood and Excelsior.
Well, their right foot. They'd come down on the right foot. Step off with their right foot.

From that on, you see. Because that's where the drummer would see the snare drummer, they'd have to see the snare drummer play with the beat. He would be set to beat, you see. When that bass drummer hit that bass drum, and that snare drummer's rolling, you see. And when they put their foot down, and they start, when they come down, they beat there. And it was wonderful just to look at them marching while they playing.
Now you see a drummer marching one step on their left, one on their right.

Now they're on the sidewalk, he got good, and come back and get them and all that. I mean, of course, I mean, they're keeping up the tradition in a way. But I mean, the assembly is not the same as it was then.
They don't have the same discipline?
